claims.quote: Our successors of the not distant future will surely succeed.
claims.description: The popular view that people will soon achieve mechanical flight, which the writer sets out and then argues against.

claims.quote: The hundred and fifty pounds of dead weight which the manager of the machine must add to it over and above that necessary in the bird may well prove an insurmountable obstacle to success.
claims.description: The added weight of a human pilot may make a man-carrying flying machine impossible.

claims.quote: It may certainly seem singular if man is never to discover any combination of substances which, under the influence of some such agency as an electric current, shall expand and contract like a muscle.
claims.description: Artificial muscle materials that expand and contract when an electric current is applied, though not expected soon.

claims.quote: May not our mechanicians, in like manner, be ultimately forced to admit that aerial flight is one of that great class of problems with which man can never cope, and give up all attempts to grapple with it?
claims.description: Mechanical flight may turn out to be permanently impossible, like squaring the circle.

claims.quote: We are peering into the law of gravitation itself with the full hope of discovering something in its origin which may enable us to evade its action.
claims.description: Science may discover the cause of gravity and find a way to escape its pull.

claims.quote: When we can produce the latter, and when the mutual action can be controlled, then may gravitation be overcome and then may men build, not merely airships, but ships which shall fly above the air, and transport their passengers from continent to continent with the speed of the celestial motions.
claims.description: Controlling the interaction between ether and matter could overcome gravity, allowing antigravity ships that fly above the atmosphere between continents at astronomical speeds.

claims.quote: Quite possibly the gates at which he is beating are, in the very nature of things, incapable of being opened.
claims.description: The nature of the ether and the cause of gravity may be forever beyond human discovery.

claims.quote: Still, considering mere possibilities, it is not impossible that the twentieth century may be destined to make known natural forces which will enable us to fly from continent to continent with a speed far exceeding that of the bird.
claims.description: Newly discovered natural forces might allow intercontinental flight far faster than a bird.

claims.quote: A plane ten feet square, for example, would not need any great inclination, nor would it require a speed higher than a few hundred feet a second to bear a man.
claims.description: A ten-foot-square wing surface moving at a few hundred feet per second could lift a man.

claims.quote: That this difficulty is insurmountable would seem to be a very fair deduction, not only from the failure of all attempts to surmount it, but from the fact that Maxim has never, so far as we are aware, followed up his seemingly successful experiment.
claims.description: A fast aeroplane can never solve stopping, landing safely and surviving engine failure, which would always be fatal.

claims.quote: A nearly horizontal surface, swinging around in a circle, on a vertical axis, like the wings of a windmill moving horizontally, will fulfil all the conditions.
claims.description: A helicopter-type machine lifted by horizontally spinning blades, perhaps two sets turning in opposite directions.

claims.quote: It follows that the smaller the machine the greater its advantage, and the smallest possible flying-machine will be the first one to be successful.
claims.description: Because weight grows faster than wing area with size, the first successful flying machines will be very small ones.

claims.quote: Now, suppose that an inventor succeeds, as well he may, in making a machine which would go into a watch-case, yet complete in all its parts, able to fly around the room.
claims.description: A watch-sized miniature flying machine that can fly around a room carrying a button, like a micro-drone.

claims.quote: If the watch-maker can make a machine which will fly through the room with a button, then, by combining ten thousand such machines he may be able to carry a man.
claims.description: Linking thousands of small flying machines together could lift a person, like a multi-rotor craft.

claims.quote: If, therefore, we are ever to have aerial navigation with our present knowledge of natural capabilities, it is to the airship floating in the air, rather than the flying-machine resting on the air, to which we are to look.
claims.description: Practical air travel, if it comes, will use lighter-than-air airships rather than heavier-than-air flying machines.

claims.quote: he might find the result to be, ideally at least, a ship which would be driven through the air by a steam-engine with a velocity far exceeding that of the fleetest Atlantic liner.
claims.description: A giant steam-driven airship at least 200 feet across and four or five times as long, perhaps built of thin steel plates, could fly faster than the fastest ocean liner.

claims.quote: Even if a dirigible balloon should cross the Atlantic, it does not follow that it could compete with the steamship in carrying passengers and freight.
claims.description: Even a transatlantic airship may not be able to compete commercially with steamships for passengers and freight.

claims.quote: Such a project is as futile as can well be imagined; no known substance would begin to resist the necessary pressure.
claims.description: A vacuum balloon made by pumping the air out of a thin hollow shell is impossible because no known material could resist the air pressure.

claims.quote: The demonstration that no possible combination of known substances, known forms of machinery, and known forms of force can be united in a practicable machine by which men shall fly long distances through the air, seems to the writer as complete as it is possible for the demonstration of any physical fact to be.
claims.description: Practical long-distance human flight is impossible with any known materials, machinery or power sources.

claims.quote: But let us discover a substance a hundred times as strong as steel, and with that some form of force hitherto unsuspected which will enable us to utilize this strength
claims.description: A material a hundred times stronger than steel, combined with a new kind of force, could make flying machines possible.

claims.quote: But we have every reason to believe that mere ingenious contrivances with our present means and forms of force will be as vain in the future as they have been in the past.
claims.description: Clever inventions using existing materials and power will keep failing to achieve flight.
